INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

ARTICLE 324 — POWER WITHIN THE CONSTITUTION, NOT POWER ABOVE IT

Credit: Y. Shivam — YouTube
[Watch the source video]
(https://t.co/YRIHmfUULR)

The central question raised by this video is fundamental:

How far does the Election Commission’s power under Article 324 extend—and where does constitutional accountability begin?

The video argues that the Election Commission is a powerful constitutional institution, but that its powers cannot be understood as unlimited or independent of Parliament-made election laws and constitutional safeguards. 

That question has acquired immediate significance.

On 5 October 2026, the Supreme Court heard petitions challenging the functioning of CEC Gyanesh Kumar and allegations that certain SIR-related decisions were taken without the concurrence of the other Election Commissioners. The Court declined to immediately suspend the CEC, but issued notices and sought the relevant records. 

The Court also made an important clarification concerning Form 6: it said that it had not approved modifications to the form and indicated that, once the records are produced, it wants to know who made the modification. 

But allegations are still allegations.

The video itself acknowledges that the claim that the CEC acted without the formal consent of the other two Commissioners has not yet been proved as a fact. 

That is precisely why constitutional democracy requires records, hearings and judicial scrutiny—not premature conclusions.

The video makes another important civic point: Article 324 gives the ECI substantial supervisory, directional and controlling powers, but those powers operate within the constitutional and statutory framework. 

And the Court's position on 5 October was equally significant: it indicated that if an ECI decision is ultimately found to be contrary to law, the Court can annul it. 

So the real democratic question is not:

“Who will win—the Supreme Court or the Election Commission?”

It is:

CAN EVERY CONSTITUTIONAL INSTITUTION BE HELD WITHIN THE LIMITS OF THE CONSTITUTION?

Because democracy does not depend merely on elections taking place.

It depends on:

FAIR ELECTORAL ROLLS.
LAWFUL PROCEDURES.
COLLECTIVE INSTITUTIONAL DECISION-MAKING.
TRANSPARENT RECORDS.
JUDICIAL REVIEW.
AND THE PROTECTION OF EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTER.

The video rightly ends on a powerful idea: constitutional literacy prevents citizens from becoming passive spectators. It urges citizens to ask whether the governing election laws were followed, whether affected voters received the legally prescribed notice and opportunity of hearing, and whether decisions were taken through the legally required institutional process. 

ARTICLE 324 IS A SHIELD FOR DEMOCRACY—
NOT A BLANK CHEQUE.

NO INSTITUTION ABOVE THE CONSTITUTION.
NO POWER ABOVE THE LAW.
NO VOTER OUTSIDE THE PROTECTION OF DEMOCRACY. 🇮🇳

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

text:
The debate surrounding #Starlink in #India is not really about internet speeds, rural connectivity or even Elon Musk.

It is about #sovereignty 
History teaches us that nations rarely lose strategic autonomy overnight. More often, dependence develops gradually through systems, networks and institutions that become too important to function without.

The #BritishEastIndiaCompany did not arrive in India as a conquering army. It arrived as a commercial enterprise promising trade, access to global markets and economic opportunity. Over time, commercial influence evolved into political leverage, strategic control and eventually colonial rule.

The world of the 21st century is different, but the underlying principle remains relevant.

Today, influence is exercised not only through territory and military power but through data, communications infrastructure, digital platforms, satellite networks and technological dependence.

This is where Starlink becomes a strategic question rather than merely a telecommunications project.

Supporters correctly point out that satellite internet can transform connectivity in remote regions, improve disaster response and bridge digital divides. These are real benefits.

However, strategic planners must also ask a different set of questions:
“Who controls the network?
Who ultimately decides where service is available?”

What happens during a geopolitical crisis?
Can a sovereign nation guarantee uninterrupted access if the infrastructure is owned, operated and controlled by a foreign private entity?

The Ukraine conflict offers a powerful example.
Reports revealed that Starlink services were restricted during a planned Ukrainian operation targeting Russian naval assets near Crimea. The result was that the operation could not proceed as intended because the communications network required for execution was unavailable.

Regardless of one’s views on the decision, the larger geopolitical lesson is clear:
A private company and its leadership possessed the ability to influence the operational options available to a sovereign state during an active conflict.

That reality should concern every serious strategic planner in the world.
The issue is not whether Elon Musk was right or wrong.

The issue is whether any nation should place critical national communications infrastructure in a position where ultimate operational control rests outside its sovereign authority.

For India, this question carries even greater significance.

India faces an increasingly contested security environment stretching from the Himalayas to the Indian Ocean. #Communications resilience is not merely an economic requirement; it is a #nationalsecurity necessity.

This does not mean rejecting foreign technology.
India has benefited enormously from international investment, technology partnerships and global integration.

But integration should never become dependence.
The ideal outcome is not isolation but strategic balance: encouraging innovation while ensuring robust regulatory oversight, #dataprotection, local compliance requirements and #sovereigncontrol mechanisms.

The lesson of the #EastIndiaCompany is often misunderstood.
The danger was never trade itself.

The danger was allowing critical leverage to accumulate outside Indian control.

As technology becomes the new arena of geopolitical competition, nations must remember a simple principle:
Infrastructure creates dependence.
Dependence creates leverage.
Leverage creates influence.

And influence, if left unchecked, can eventually challenge sovereignty itself.

India was colonised once through commerce and influence.
The next challenge, if it ever comes, will not arrive on sailing ships.

It will arrive through networks, platforms, satellites and systems that become too important to question

That is why the Starlink debate is not merely abt connectivity.
It is about ensuring that 🇮🇳’s digital future remains firmly under Indian sovereign control #JaiHind

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

Last week I saved a man’s life. He’s 77 years old and a good close friend of mine. He was declining after he lost the charging device to his insulin pump. I saw it coming a week ahead of time and asked him what I was supposed to do if he fell and didn’t have his phone. He didn’t have an answer. He had fallen in his garage. He had fallen by his pool. I called every morning to make sure he was ok. 

One morning I called and he didn’t answer. Then I called later that day and it went straight to voicemail which told me his phone didn’t get charged. I decided if I couldn’t get ahold of him the next morning I would call the police. Fortunately that next morning, he answered. 

A few days later however, he answered my morning call from his kitchen floor. He had been there since the day before. Why he didn’t call someone would become apparent later. He told me, if I can just get some fluids I’ll be ok. I told him I would have Jenny call for help. He disconnected the call. Jenny called the police and they sent the paramedics and he went to the hospital. 

He had emergency surgery to remove his inflamed gallbladder then was in the ICU for a few days. He has since been move to a physical therapy facility to be rehabilitated. 

He once told me, “when I die, you’ll be a very wealthy man”

When it came down to it, I saved his life.

text:
Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

text:
Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

A road safety officer stopped us today. My brother was driving, and he presented his valid UAE/Dubai driving licence. The vehicle papers were checked everything was intact. Fire extinguisher? Intact. Warning triangle? Intact. Spare tyre? Intact.

The officer then demanded a Nigerian driver's licence. My brother explained that we don't reside in Nigeria and had only just returned. The officer insisted that a Dubai licence could not be used in Nigeria, even for one day.

I simply asked him to show us the specific law we had violated. Instead of showing the law, the attitude changed. He started saying I was claiming to know everything and that "this is Nigeria."

I also explained that my own Nigerian driver's licence has expired because I no longer drive in Nigeria. I told him I have not driven since I returned and have no intention of renewing a licence for a vehicle I am not driving. He insisted that even if I don't drive, I must renew it.

I asked him: Why should I keep spending money renewing a driver's licence when I have decided not to drive in Nigeria? And why are citizens constantly being suffocated with one charge, renewal or demand after another?

I even asked whether he understood that citizens have constitutional rights and should not be treated as if every interaction with a government officer must end in intimidation or payment. He simply looked at me as though I was the one who had lost my mind.

What made it worse was seeing a condemned truck that clearly should not have been on the road pass right in front of us without being stopped, while we were being held over a valid foreign driver's licence.

When I questioned the double standard, the situation escalated. I made a phone call, and the officer accused me of calling "cultists" to attack them.

The next thing, a JTF team comprising soldiers, police and civil defence arrived aggressively, shouting for everyone to come down from the vehicle. We were three people—my brother, his wife and me. His wife was still inside the vehicle.

They aggressively tried to take my phone when I was recording what was happening. I asked them to first hear our side of the story.

After they eventually listened and confirmed what had happened, we were told to leave and not be aggressive towards officers. But I never came there looking for trouble. I was simply asking questions and trying to document what was happening to us.

They later insisted that I delete the video, which I did in their presence.

Why all this suffocation of citizens?

Why must asking a legitimate question to a government officer suddenly become "insulting an officer," "knowing too much," or "challenging authority"?

Respect for citizens and respect for personnel must work both ways. A uniform is not a licence to intimidate citizens, and citizens should not have to surrender their rights simply because someone in uniform says, "This is Nigeria."

Say NO to citizens' intimidation.

I will never bow to intimidation or oppression.

Yesterday I got a bit roasted on X because I said my agent checks me in for my flights, so let me double down: it also helps me book basically every plane ticket.

I just landed in India and they asked for one of those crazy health/immigration forms with passport info, where you’re staying, flight details, etc. I sent it to my agent, it filled everything out, great job, I went back to reading my book.

A bunch of people replied: “I’m a competent adult, I know how to do this, I don’t need AI.”

Which is totally fair. Do whatever works for you! 

I also know how to wash dishes and I love my dishwasher. I know how to write a letter, put it in an envelope and go to the post office, and yet I prefer email. I know how to do mental arithmetic and I still use a calculator.

The point of technology is very rarely that humans are incapable of doing the thing. It’s that our time and attention are better spent somewhere else.

Instead of spending 20 minutes fighting with a PDF, finding my passport number, hotel address and flight information in five different places, I can read my book. Instead of manually replying to three emails just to send my landlord some insurance information, an agent can handle it and I get another 20 minutes with my 18-month-old daughter, Josephine.

I think people underestimate AI agents for two reasons.

First, capitalism has this amazing tendency to take things that were once reserved for rich people and, through technology and scale, give them to everyone. Rich people have had executive assistants forever. Someone books their flights and restaurants, coordinates meetings, answers routine communications, fills out paperwork, reminds them what they forgot. AI is going to give some version of that to billions of people.

Second, a huge amount of economic progress is simply removing friction. Coase would call a lot of this transaction costs. One form takes 15 minutes, one email takes 3 minutes, one reservation takes 10 minutes. None of these things individually feels revolutionary, but remove thousands of them over a lifetime and it compounds into something enormous.

So yes, I am perfectly capable of checking myself into a flight but now I just don’t see why I should.

quotedTweet.text:
I’m a competent adult. Why do I need an “AI agent” to check into a flight for me? 

I’m literate. Why do I need an “AI agent” to read and write emails for me? Also, I don’t get so many emails that I can’t answer them myself. 

The reason “no one uses AI” is that there’s no serious utility here for the vast majority of people.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
NIA Arrests Another Absconding Accused in Praveen Nettaru Murder Case

New Delhi, 6th Aug, 2026

The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Wednesday arrested another key absconding accused in the 2022 murder of Karnataka BJP leader Praveen Nettaru, taking the total number of arrests in the high-profile case to 25.

The accused, identified as Ummar Farook M.R., was apprehended from Kochi, Kerala following a targeted operation based on credible intelligence inputs.

Ummar Farook, an absconding accused had a Red Corner Notice (RCN) and a non-bailable warrant for arrest against him. The investigating agency had also announced a reward of ₹4 lakh for information leading to his arrest.

The NIA had earlier chargesheeted Ummar Farook in connection with the conspiracy behind the murder under various provisions of the Indian Penal Code and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. Investigations revealed that he attended a conspiracy meeting at the office of the banned Popular Front of India (PFI) in Sullia town along with other accused.

Investigation revealed that Ummar Farook had agreed to provide his motorcycle to a co-accused for identifying potential targets and conducting reconnaissance in Bellare village before the murder. He is also accused of participating along with other co-accused persons in an attempt to eliminate a protected witness in the case.

The latest arrest comes weeks after the NIA, in July this year, apprehended two other absconding accused—Abdul Nasir P. alias Nasir, and Naushad—from Kochi in Kerala and Hosur in Tamil Nadu, respectively, in a coordinated operation based on information received from the Andhra Pradesh Police.

The murder of Praveen Nettaru, a local BJP leader from Dakshina Kannada district, on 26th July, 2022 had triggered widespread outrage and led to the NIA taking over the investigation. NIA probe has revealed that the killing was part of a larger criminal conspiracy orchestrated by cadres of the banned PFI.

In  this case, two accused remain absconding. Efforts are continuing to trace and arrest the remaining absconding accused and to bring the investigation to its logical conclusion.

text:
Why should we not stay in India anymore?

I recently had a terrifying experience on the night of 25th September 2026 during Ganesh Utsav, that I feel compelled to share it.

While attending the Utsav, my iPhone was stolen from my pocket near Nagarkar Talim Chowk on Laxmi Road at around 10:30 PM IST. I was alert, and the moment it was taken, I immediately realized that someone had removed it from my pocket. I checked with the people around me, but the phone was already gone.

I immediately rushed to the nearest police station, Vishrambaug Police Station, where I filed an FIR. After getting a duplicate SIM card issued, I also had my IMEI number blocked.

However, I did not lose hope. I continued trying to find ways to track my device on my own. As part of this effort, I even visited several police stations to check whether they had caught any thieves from whom my phone might have been recovered. Unfortunately, I had no luck.

Then, while all of this was going on, I received two SMS messages on my registered number from the thief. The messages claimed that my phone had been located and provided a link supposedly allowing me to track its location. I immediately recognized it as a phishing attempt.

I went to the nearest police station to report this, hoping that this new information might actually help track the person who had stolen my phone. Instead, I was told to go back to the police station where I had originally filed my FIR.

So I went back to Vishrambaug Police Station. They gave me the numbers of two police officers and asked me to contact them. I did exactly that. But after explaining the entire situation, I was told the same thing I already knew: “This is a fake link. Don’t click on it.”

And that was it.

No further assistance. No attempt to investigate the phone number. No effort to use the information I had provided. Nothing…

I thought about it for a while and realized that perhaps the Maharashtra Cyber Police could help. I had the thief's phone number, and I assumed that a cyber crime department would have the necessary resources and technology to trace the number and potentially locate the device or identify the person behind it.

So I traveled to Shivajinagar, where the Maharashtra Cyber Police headquarters are located. There, I was told to contact the Rural Cyber Police because I live in a rural area.

I then traveled to the Rural Cyber Cell. And guess what I was told there? “Your FIR is with Pune Police, so you need to check with them.”

At this point, I had gone from one police station to another, from one department to another, carrying the same information and explaining the same situation repeatedly.

And after going through all of this, I realized just how helpless an ordinary taxpayer can feel when they actually need the system to work. I have paid taxes for years. I have followed the law. I did exactly what a responsible citizen is supposed to do, yet when I actually needed assistance, there was no coordination.

One department directed me to another. One police station directed me to another. Officials repeated information that I already knew instead of acting on the new information I was providing. There appeared to be no clear ownership of the case and no one willing to take responsibility for actually pursuing it.
What is the point of filing an FIR and registering on CEIR portal, when new and potentially useful information emerges, the victim is simply sent from one department to another?

And where is the technology that should allow law enforcement to act quickly in cases like this?
The most frustrating part is that I wasn't asking anyone to perform a miracle. I wasn't asking for special treatment. I was asking for basic assistance after becoming a victim of a crime.

Instead, I spent my time travelling between police stations, departments and offices, repeatedly explaining the same situation, while everyone seemed more interested in telling me who was not responsible rather than figuring out who was.

This experience has left me extremely disappointed and angry.

A common taxpayer should not have to become an investigator, case coordinator and police liaison just to get basic assistance after their phone is stolen. If this is what a citizen has to go through even after immediately reporting a crime and providing potentially useful information, then something is seriously wrong with the system.

I understood if any important person's son or daughter phone would have been stolen in the same way, these department would have worked very differently and the phone would probably be recovered within days but unfortunately we are just a common middle class man who does have any power nor have anyone's help. We are just money printing machine for the Indian government.

Dealing this situation made me realized how bad India is, why we should not stay in this country.

text:
WHEN POWER FEARS WOMEN WHO SPEAK, DEMOCRACY IS ALREADY IN DANGER

Neha Bora is not merely a face in a protest.

She represents something far more uncomfortable for those in power—a young citizen who refuses to accept that questioning authority is an offence.

The struggle at Jantar Mantar is ultimately not just about one protest, one Election Commission decision, or one political demand.

It is about a much larger question:

Can citizens question institutions of power without being intimidated, detained or silenced?

The material in this video raises deeply disturbing allegations about the treatment of women protesters and women journalists by police personnel—including allegations of manhandling and sexual harassment. These allegations must be investigated impartially, with evidence, CCTV footage and due process—not dismissed, buried or converted into a political blame game.

And when a journalist says she spent hours at a police station attempting to have her complaint registered, the question becomes even more serious: does the rule of law protect the citizen first, or the uniform first?

Neha Bora's resistance therefore deserves to be understood beyond party politics.

She is asking questions about electoral democracy.

She is questioning institutional accountability.

She is standing with citizens who fear losing their voice in the electoral process.

And she is refusing to accept that the police, the administration or any constitutional institution should become beyond scrutiny.

A democracy does not become strong because citizens obey.

A democracy becomes strong because citizens are free to question.

If the authorities believe the protesters are wrong, answer them.

If the Election Commission believes its actions are lawful, explain them transparently.

If the police believe their conduct was lawful, let an independent investigation establish the facts.

But do not silence the questioner merely because the question is inconvenient.

The answer to dissent cannot be intimidation.

The answer to journalism cannot be harassment.

The answer to democratic protest cannot be fear.

And the answer to a citizen demanding accountability cannot be—“Know your place.”

Neha Bora and every citizen exercising the democratic right to question power deserve something very simple:

Dignity. Due process. Accountability. And the freedom to speak.

This resistance is not against India.

It is for an India where no office is bigger than the Constitution, no institution is above scrutiny, and no citizen is too small to question power.

Let the evidence speak.
Let independent investigation speak.
Let the Constitution speak.
And let the people speak.

Because democracy survives not when power becomes unquestionable—but when citizens remain unafraid to question it.

Full statement of @DrSJaishankar in the Rajya Sabha today 
On Bangladesh 

*Statement by EAM in the Rajya Sabha* 

Mr. Chairman Sir,

I rise to apprise this august House of certain recent developments pertaining to Bangladesh. As Hon’ble Members are aware, India-Bangladesh relations have been exceptionally close for many decades over many governments. Concern about recent violence and instability there is shared across the political spectrum. 

2.Since the election in January 2024, there has been considerable tensions, deep divides and growing polarization in Bangladesh politics. This underlying foundation aggravated a student agitation that started in June this year. There was growing violence, including attacks on public buildings and infrastructure, as well as traffic and rail obstructions. The violence continued through the month of July. Throughout this period, we repeatedly counselled restraint and urged that the situation be defused through dialogue. Similar urgings were made to various political forces with whom we were in touch.

3.Sir, despite a Supreme Court judgement on 21 July, there was no let-up in the public agitation. Various decisions and actions taken thereafter only exacerbated the situation. The agitation at this stage coalesced around a one-point agenda, that is that the Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina should step down. 

4.On 4th August, events took a very serious turn. Attacks on police, including police stations and government installations, intensified even as overall levels of violence greatly escalated. Properties of individuals associated with the regime were torched across the country. What was particularly worrying was that minorities, their businesses and temples also came under attack at multiple locations. The full extent of this is still not clear. 

5.Sir, On 5th August, demonstrators converged in Dhaka despite the curfew. Our understanding is that after a meeting with leaders of the security establishment, Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina apparently made the decision to resign. At very short notice, she requested approval to come for the moment to India. We simultaneously received a request for flight clearance from Bangladesh authorities. She arrived yesterday evening in Delhi. 

6.The situation in Bangladesh Sir, is still evolving. The Army Chief, General Waker-uz-Zaman, addressed the nation on 5th August. He spoke about assuming responsibility and constituting an interim government.

7.We are in close and continuous touch with the Indian community in Bangladesh through our diplomatic missions. There are an estimated 19,000 Indian nationals there, of which about 9,000 are students. The bulk of the students have already returned to India in the month of July on the advice of the High Commission. In terms of our diplomatic presence, in addition to the High Commission in Dhaka, we have Assistant High Commissions in Chittagong, Rajshahi, Khulna and Sylhet. It is our expectation that the host government will provide the required security protection for these establishments. We look forward to their normal functioning once the situation stabilizes.

8.Chairman Sir, we are also monitoring the situation with regard to the status of minorities. There are reports of initiatives by various groups and organizations to ensure their protection and well-being. We welcome that, but will naturally remain deeply concerned till law and order is visibly restored. Our border guarding forces have also been instructed to be exceptionally alert in view of this complex situation.

I seek the understanding and support of the House in regard to sensitive issues regarding an important neighbour on which there has always been strong national consensus.

text:
Meta told to disable ‘child sex abuse’ content

Instagram asked to provide explanation in seven days; ‘action’ to be decided after reviewing reply

IT Act, 2000, penalises obscene material; the IT Rules, 2021, enforce obligations on social media

Social media firms in breach may lose exemption under the law for third-party information or data

The Hindu Bureau NEW DELHI

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has directed Meta, the parent body of several social media platforms, to disable advertisements and content promoting and facilitating access to child sexual exploitative and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram, according to government sources.

It has also sought an explanation on the issue.

“The Ministry has ordered Instagram to disable such advertisements. The government has also demanded a detailed explanation on the action taken and other relevant information within seven days. A notice in this regard was issued on Saturday,” said a source.

It is learnt that the notice was sent following a directive from IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw to senior Ministry officials. Further course of action will be decided after reviewing the reply, said the source.

Policy and standards

The move came a day after the BBC Eye published its investigation revealing that Instagram had allegedly been running “paid adverts promoting child sexual abuse material in India” and that such advertisements linked users to channels on Telegram, where they could buy the material.

Meta’s policy on advertisements, meanwhile, stipulate that their content must comply with community standards and must not have imagery depicting nudity and activities that are sexual or sexually suggestive.

In response to a query on the notice, a Meta spokesperson pointed to an earlier statement shared after the BBC report came out, where Meta said it had a “zero tolerance policy for soliciting or sharing CSEAM” and added that while the company deployed technology to detect such advertisements, it was in a “constant battle with criminals who hide among 3.5 billion users and try to evade our detection”. 

According to Meta’s policy, advertisements must “comply with the community standards on adult nudity and sexual activity. Ads must not contain imagery depicting nudity, sexual activity, depictions of people in explicit or sexually suggestive positions, or activities that are sexually suggestive”.

Rules and punishments

The policy sets additional restrictions beyond the Community Standard on Adult Nudity and Sexual Activity, says its sub-site.

According to a written reply by Mr. Vaishnaw to the Lok Sabha last year, the IT Act, 2000 provides punishment for publishing or transmitting obscene material and material containing sexually explicit acts in electronic form.

The Act also provides for stringent punishment for publishing or transmitting material depicting children in sexually explicit acts in electronic form.

Besides, the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 enforces obligations on the intermediaries, including social media intermediaries, to observe due diligence.

If they fail to observe it, they lose the exemption under law for third-party information or data or communication links hosted by them. The intermediaries are required to remove any such content within 24 hours.

The Ministry of Home Affairs operates the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal to receive complaints against cybercrimes, with special focus on cybercrimes against children.

It has also set up the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) for such crimes.

The government has, from time to time, blocked websites containing CSAM, based on lists from Interpol received through the Central Bureau of Investigation. It has issued an order to Internet Service Providers (ISPs), directing them to block access to such web pages or websites, said the reply.

text:
Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

text:
Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

I swiftly responded to MeitY on 19th March at 4:16 AM enquiring the cause that led to this removal under section 69A. ( Haven’t received any response yet )

Next I consulted with @NakulGandhi511 upon the recommendation of @iArpitSpeaks as he had earlier met with similar fate and got his account back.

Nakul sir guided me for a week and introduced me with @apar1984 who runs @internetfreedom . 

He took over my case pro bono ( for free ) and guided me accordingly. 

On 1st of April I finally filed my writ petition. The notary, wakalatnama was all new to me coz I had never been in court till this date but barring that I had to do nothing. 

Every response, every draft was given to me by @namanbasoyaa who works with Apar sir. 

I got my listing on 6th of April with the honr Judge Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. 

He didn’t even waste 10 mins and ordered a restore provided that the posts that warranted an action against me shall stay unblocked until the committee level hearing of MeitY ( It’s not scheduled yet )

In fact I still don’t have the blocking order that necessitated such an action against me that is ultra vires of the constitution. Section 69A doesn’t permit govt to remove pre-emotive post based on speculation and that’s exactly what govt effectively did by withholding my entire account not some posts. 

Also big thanks to my followers who stood with me. Some used VPN just to stay connected. I’m indebted to all of you and IFF and Apar sir in particular. 

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for. 

May better sense prevails. Peace ✌🏽

No specific statute or rule in Indian law expressly authorises or bans a government institution from blocking a citizen on its official social media handle. Such blocks follow the platform’s terms of service, available to any account.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo
